author: blu
body: A caution the names do not show: read-file is ALSO a compiler builtin that reads the serial port, and at an application site the builtin wins over the effect op. A `with FileSystem` handler over read-file would discharge the row at type level while the call went to serial at runtime. read-text exists because of that: it is a pure effect op, absent from the builtin tables, so a bare read-text always reaches the handler that services it. A layer that holds the block device services read-text and write-file over the disk and re-emits [Device.Block]; the program above it carries FileSystem.Read and never block access. That is the attenuation: holding FileSystem does not grant the disk.

author: blu
body: The compiler installs these two functions as the DEFAULT handler for read-text and write-file when a program performs a FileSystem op with no `with` of its own. A hand-emitted stub checks the program's cap-filesystem-read / cap-filesystem-write bit, sets the kernel fs-elevated cell so the block device answers even though the program holds only FileSystem.Read and never Device.Block, calls one of these, and clears the cell. The DIRECTION bit is enforced by that stub; the path SCOPE is enforced by fat16 itself (fat16-scope-admits). So a program granted FileSystem.Read that performs write-file is refused at the stub, which is the guarantee this makes real: holding FileSystem does not grant the disk, and holding it read-only does not grant a write.

author: blu
body: This is why FileSystem cites Fat16: the default filesystem IS fat16, and a program that cites the effect must carry the backend that services it. These functions are called only from the compiler-emitted stub (by name, over the handler table), never from Codex source, so their Device.Block row is discharged by the elevation, not by the program above them.
